transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Um, well, my manager at the restaurant actually told me I needed to come in, or at least he strongly suggested I take some time off and see someone after what happened on Tuesday. Or maybe it was Wednesday? No, it was definitely Tuesday because it was the lunch rush and we had the chicken salad special, which always brings in a huge crowd from the office park across the street. 

I've been waitressing for a while to pay the bills, you know, since I took a break from my classes, and I'm usually really good at keeping everything straight in my head. Multitasking is usually my thing. But lately... well, what really scared everyone at work, and I mean really freaked out my manager Dave, is that I just started freezing up. Right in the middle of service. Like, the restaurant is completely packed, people are waving me down for extra ranch or drink refills, and I just stop moving. 

I've been doing things totally out of order, too, which makes no sense. Like, the other day, I was supposed to be cashing out table four. They were in a hurry. But instead of closing their check, I just walked over to the soda station. I was just standing there by the Diet Coke dispenser for I don't even know how long, and I had the cash drawer key in my hand—I was holding it so tight my knuckles were white—and I just kept repeating table numbers out loud. Just saying, "Table four, table seven, table nine," over and over to myself. I wasn't getting their drinks, I wasn't opening the register, I wasn't doing anything I was supposed to be doing. Dave had to come over and physically tap my shoulder to snap me out of it, and he looked really spooked. I just... I get stuck, I guess? And my brain is trying to do the steps but my body isn't, and then I'm just standing there with a key while people are waiting for their change. So, yeah, that's why I'm here.
When you freeze up like that, do you experience any physical sensations, like a strange smell, a feeling of déjà vu, or any involuntary twitching or jerking movements?

Um, no... no, definitely nothing like that. I mean, as far as smells go, it's just the usual stuff, you know? The restaurant always smells like old fry oil and that really strong industrial lemon cleaner we use to wipe down the booths. Dave is super particular about the sanitizing buckets, so that lemon bleach smell is always kind of burned into my nose anyway. But no, no weird phantom smells out of nowhere or anything like that. 

And I'm definitely not twitching or jerking around. If anything, it's the exact opposite of that. It's like my whole body just turns to heavy cement. Like I was saying with the register key, I was gripping it so hard my hand actually cramped up later that night, but my arm wasn't shaking or spasming. It was just totally, completely locked in place. It’s almost like the connection between my brain saying 'walk to table four' and my legs actually taking a step just gets completely severed, but without any physical jerking or movement at all. 

And as for déjà vu... no, it doesn't feel like I'm reliving a memory or anything mystical like that. It's more like... like time just stretches out and I'm trapped in this one single second while the rest of the world is fast-forwarding around me. Like, I remember just staring at the clear plastic tubing on the soda machine, watching the little syrup bubbles in the Sprite line, and I'm just completely frozen there while the servers are rushing past me with huge trays of plates. So yeah, no twitching or weird smells at all, just... just that awful, heavy stuck feeling while everyone else is moving.
Did anything particularly stressful or upsetting happen in your life shortly before these freezing episodes started occurring?

Well, it's not like one big, dramatic thing just suddenly happened right before the freezing started. It's more like... like a slow buildup, you know? This whole change in me, this whole feeling of getting stuck and just not being able to do things right, it's been building for a long time. About a year and two months, actually. 

I know the exact timeline because that's when Dave—my manager—asked me to take on the evening shift lead responsibilities. It was right after Thanksgiving last year, well, a year ago last November. Our old shift lead, Sarah, she moved to Colorado because her boyfriend got a job at some tech startup out there, and she just up and left with like, two weeks' notice. So Dave was in a total bind, and he pulled me into the back office—the one that always smells like stale coffee and printer ink—and told me I was the most reliable person he had. Which was nice to hear, you know, because I do try hard. 

But taking on the shift lead thing... it was a lot. Suddenly I wasn't just worrying about my own tables. I had to manage the floor, handle customer complaints, do the cash drop at the end of the night, and make sure the side work was actually getting done, because the newer servers always try to sneak out without rolling their silverware. And it just felt like this massive weight on my shoulders, like I had to be hyper-aware of every single moving part in the restaurant all at once. 

So, yeah, that was about fourteen months ago. And at first, I thought I was handling it okay, but then I started feeling really overwhelmed, like my brain was just constantly buzzing with too much information. And then the freezing thing started happening more recently. But the whole... the whole shift in how my brain feels, that definitely traces back to when I got that promotion a year and two months ago. It just felt like too much pressure, you know? Like I was supposed to be the one holding the whole place together, and instead, I'm the one falling apart next to the soda machine.
When you are standing there frozen, do you feel like you are watching yourself from the outside, or does the world around you feel unreal or dreamlike?

Um, no, I wouldn't say it's like watching myself from the outside. I mean, I know some people talk about that, like floating above their body or something, but I'm definitely still in my body. Very much in it. Like I was saying before, it's just so heavy. I feel every ounce of that heaviness. And as for the world feeling unreal or like a dream... no, not really. It's actually almost too real, if that makes sense? 

Like, when I'm stuck there, I'm hyper-aware of everything going on around me. I'm not in a dream at all. I can see the exact color of the ketchup bottles on the tables, and I can hear the clinking of the silverware when the busboy dumps the bins into the dish pit. It's so loud. I can hear the exact conversations people are having at the booths closest to me. The other day, when I was frozen by the soda machine, I could hear this guy at table six complaining to his wife that his fries were too salty, and I could hear the exact tone of his voice, like this really whiny, nasal sound. 

So it's not like a dream where things are fuzzy or weird. It's just that I'm completely anchored to the floor while all these very real, very sharp, very loud things are happening all around me. It's like I'm the only thing that's stopped, but the restaurant is still functioning exactly how it always does. The fluorescent lights are still humming—you know that awful buzzing sound those long bulbs make when they're about to burn out? I can hear that perfectly. I can feel the sticky spot on the floor where someone spilled a Shirley Temple earlier in the shift. Everything is so incredibly real and present, it's just that I can't interact with it. I'm just trapped inside my own head, inside this heavy body, just watching all these totally normal, real-life things happen without me. So no, definitely not a dream, and definitely not an out-of-body thing. Just... just really, really stuck in the reality of the restaurant, unable to move.
During these past fourteen months, have you felt consistently down, hopeless, or lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

Well, I don't know if I'd say "hopeless," exactly, because that sounds so... I don't know, dramatic? Like people crying in movies. But definitely the lost interest part. Yeah, absolutely that. It's actually been a really huge issue at home lately. 

I used to have all these things I loved doing on my days off to decompress from the restaurant. We live about twenty minutes from the coast, and I used to love going for these long beach walks, especially in the early morning before the tourists get out there and clog up the sand. I'd look for sea glass—you know, the really smooth green and blue pieces? I had a whole mason jar of them on the kitchen windowsill. And baking, too. I used to bake all the time. I'd make sourdough, banana bread, these intricate little lemon tarts that my husband absolutely loved. I even had this little herb garden out on our back patio with basil and thyme, and I'd write in my journal every single night. I had this really nice leather-bound one with the thick paper, and I'd just fill pages and pages about my day or whatever was on my mind.

But over this past year, since all that pressure at work started... I just stopped. All of it. I don't really go for beach walks, bake, garden, or write in my journal much anymore. Actually, I don't do them at all. I look at the jar of sea glass, or the flour bin in the pantry, or the weeds completely taking over the patio, and I just... I can't. It's not even that I feel actively sad and tearful about it. It's more like this massive, heavy blankness. 

And it's really hard on my husband. He tries so hard to connect with me. He'll come home and sit down on the couch, and he'll try to talk with me about his day, or ask me about mine, or suggest we watch a show, and I mostly just sit there. I just sit there staring at the coffee table. I hear him talking, but the words just kind of wash over me, and it feels like I can’t get myself to care or start anything. The energy it would take just to open my mouth and respond, or to pick up a pen for my journal, or to get out the mixing bowls... it feels like I'm being asked to move a mountain. It’s like the starter motor in my brain is just completely broken. So he talks, and I just sit, and I don't really do much of anything at all these days.
Have you ever gone through a period like this before—where you felt this same heavy blankness and lost interest in everything—at any point earlier in your life, perhaps years ago?

No, honestly... I don't think so. I mean, I really try to think back, and I can't remember ever feeling like this before. Like, even when I was younger, back when I was taking some classes at the community college—I was taking some general business and hospitality courses, thinking maybe I'd open my own little bakery or cafe one day, since I used to love baking so much—I was always the one doing a million things at once. 

I was going to class, working a full shift at this other diner I used to work at before my current place, and I still had the energy to go out with friends or stay up late organizing my apartment. I never had this... this heavy blankness. Even when I was exhausted, it was just regular tired, you know? Like my feet would ache from being on the floor all day, but my brain was still going. I still wanted to do things. 

Even in my mid-twenties, when I first met my husband, he actually used to joke that I was like a hummingbird because I could never just sit still. I was always buzzing around, fixing up the patio, trying out new recipes, planning little weekend trips up the coast for us. I've always been a doer. I liked being busy. 

So this whole feeling of just being totally drained and disconnected, where I can't even bring myself to care about the things sitting right in front of me... it's completely new. It really just started building up after that promotion to shift lead fourteen months ago. Before that, I was totally fine. I mean, sure, everyone has bad days, right? Like if a customer screams at you over a coupon or you get a flat tire on the way to work, you feel bummed out or stressed for a day or two. But it always passed. It never stuck around and turned into this massive, paralyzing weight that just swallowed up my whole personality. So, yeah, no, I've never gone through anything even remotely like this before. This is all completely uncharted territory for me.
When you have days off from the restaurant, does this heavy, blank feeling and the inability to do things persist, or do you feel a significant sense of relief and return to your normal self?

No, it... it really doesn't go away at all. You'd think it would, right? You'd think, okay, I'm away from the restaurant, I'm away from the buzzing lights and the tickets printing and the customers complaining, so I should just bounce back and feel normal. But I don't. It persists completely. 

Like I was telling you just a minute ago about all those things I used to love? The beach walks, the baking, the gardening, writing in my journal? Those were my day-off activities. That was my whole routine when I wasn't scheduled. But now, when my day off rolls around—like, say it's a Tuesday and I have absolutely nowhere to be—I just wake up and that heavy, blank feeling is already right there, just pinning me down. I don't really go for those beach walks to find sea glass anymore. I don't bake. I don't tend to the garden, and I don't write in my journal much anymore... well, really not at all. It's just this massive wall of nothingness that follows me home. 

And it's almost worse on the days off because that's when my husband is home with me, and like I said, he tries so hard to engage. He'll sit down and try to talk with me, maybe ask what I want to do with our free time or tell me about something he read, and I mostly just sit there. I just sit on the couch because it feels like I absolutely can’t get myself to care or start anything, even on a day when I have literally zero responsibilities. The whole day just slips by. 

It's really frustrating, honestly, because you expect to feel relief on a day off. You expect to be your old self, and when you aren't, when you just sit there staring at the coffee table while your husband is trying to have a normal conversation... it just really shows how stuck I am. So, no, there’s no relief. Whether I'm at the diner or at home on a Sunday, it’s just the same heavy blankness.

In your entire life, have you ever experienced a period of several days or weeks where you felt unusually energetic, didn't need much sleep, or felt so 'up' or hyperactive that it was noticeable to others?

No, I don't... no. I’ve always been someone who really, really needs their sleep. Like, if I don't get at least seven or eight hours, I am just useless the next day. Even back when I was doing those community college classes and working full-time at the other diner, I still slept. I mean, I might have stayed up late a few nights here and there, maybe organizing the apartment, like I mentioned before—I used to have this whole system for my baking supplies, where I'd put all the different flours and sugars into these glass airtight containers and make these cute little chalkboard labels for them so everything looked perfect in the pantry. But even when I did that, I was still exhausted the next day. I'd be dragging my feet through my shift, drinking like three or four cups of black coffee just to keep my eyes open while I was rolling silverware at the back station. 

I never had a time where I just didn't need sleep, or where I felt perfectly fine running on empty. And as for being unusually energetic or, like, hyper... I mean, I was a busy person, sure. Like I said, my husband called me a hummingbird because I liked getting things done. But it wasn't... it wasn't weird or abnormal, you know? It wasn't like I was bouncing off the walls or talking so fast people couldn't understand me. I was just productive. I'd wake up, go to the farmer's market early on a Sunday to get the best heirloom tomatoes and fresh basil from this one specific vendor before they sold out, and then I'd come home and make bruschetta for us... but it was just normal life energy. It wasn't some kind of crazy high where everyone was staring at me. So, no, I've never experienced anything like what you're describing. Never.

It's like I'm the only thing that's stopped, but the restaurant is still functioning exactly how it always does. The fluorescent lights are still humming—you know that awful buzzing sound those long bulbs make when they're about to burn out? I can hear that perfectly. I can feel the sticky spot on the floor where someone spilled a Shirley Temple earlier in the shift. Everything is so incredibly real and present, it's just that I can't interact with it. I'm just trapped inside my own head, inside this heavy body, just watching all these totally normal, real-life things happen without me. So no, definitely not a dream, and definitely not an out-of-body thing. Just... just really, really stuck in the reality of the restaurant, unable to move.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between adjustment disorders with anxiety (F43.22) or mixed anxiety and depression (F43.23) and other conditions by assessing for depressed mood.
doctor.question: During these past fourteen months, have you felt consistently down, hopeless, or lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I don’t really go for beach walks, bake, garden, or write in my journal much anymore, and when my husband tries to talk with me I mostly just sit there because it feels like I can’t get myself to care or start anything.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in previously enjoyed activities, which corresponds to the negative symptoms characterized by diminished motivation and social interest.

patient.answer:
Well, I don't know if I'd say "hopeless," exactly, because that sounds so... I don't know, dramatic? Like people crying in movies. But definitely the lost interest part. Yeah, absolutely that. It's actually been a really huge issue at home lately. 

I used to have all these things I loved doing on my days off to decompress from the restaurant. We live about twenty minutes from the coast, and I used to love going for these long beach walks, especially in the early morning before the tourists get out there and clog up the sand. I'd look for sea glass—you know, the really smooth green and blue pieces? I had a whole mason jar of them on the kitchen windowsill. And baking, too. I used to bake all the time. I'd make sourdough, banana bread, these intricate little lemon tarts that my husband absolutely loved. I even had this little herb garden out on our back patio with basil and thyme, and I'd write in my journal every single night. I had this really nice leather-bound one with the thick paper, and I'd just fill pages and pages about my day or whatever was on my mind.

But over this past year, since all that pressure at work started... I just stopped. All of it. I don't really go for beach walks, bake, garden, or write in my journal much anymore. Actually, I don't do them at all. I look at the jar of sea glass, or the flour bin in the pantry, or the weeds completely taking over the patio, and I just... I can't. It's not even that I feel actively sad and tearful about it. It's more like this massive, heavy blankness. 

And it's really hard on my husband. He tries so hard to connect with me. He'll come home and sit down on the couch, and he'll try to talk with me about his day, or ask me about mine, or suggest we watch a show, and I mostly just sit there. I just sit there staring at the coffee table. I hear him talking, but the words just kind of wash over me, and it feels like I can’t get myself to care or start anything. The energy it would take just to open my mouth and respond, or to pick up a pen for my journal, or to get out the mixing bowls... it feels like I'm being asked to move a mountain. It’s like the starter motor in my brain is just completely broken. So he talks, and I just sit, and I don't really do much of anything at all these days.

inference.note: The patient's description of persistent 'heavy blankness,' anhedonia (loss of interest in hobbies), and executive dysfunction ('starter motor' being broken) over 14 months strongly suggests a depressive component, moving the focus toward mood disorders (F32/F33) while retaining adjustment disorder (F43.2) as a differential given the clear stressor.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced these symptoms of low mood and loss of interest in a prior, distinct episode in her life, which would distinguish between single-episode (F32.9) and recurrent (F33.9) major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever gone through a period like this before—where you felt this same heavy blankness and lost interest in everything—at any point earlier in your life, perhaps years ago?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a past history of depressive episodes or similar periods of blankness earlier in life, which is not covered by the current symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, honestly... I don't think so. I mean, I really try to think back, and I can't remember ever feeling like this before. Like, even when I was younger, back when I was taking some classes at the community college—I was taking some general business and hospitality courses, thinking maybe I'd open my own little bakery or cafe one day, since I used to love baking so much—I was always the one doing a million things at once. 

I was going to class, working a full shift at this other diner I used to work at before my current place, and I still had the energy to go out with friends or stay up late organizing my apartment. I never had this... this heavy blankness. Even when I was exhausted, it was just regular tired, you know? Like my feet would ache from being on the floor all day, but my brain was still going. I still wanted to do things. 

Even in my mid-twenties, when I first met my husband, he actually used to joke that I was like a hummingbird because I could never just sit still. I was always buzzing around, fixing up the patio, trying out new recipes, planning little weekend trips up the coast for us. I've always been a doer. I liked being busy. 

So this whole feeling of just being totally drained and disconnected, where I can't even bring myself to care about the things sitting right in front of me... it's completely new. It really just started building up after that promotion to shift lead fourteen months ago. Before that, I was totally fine. I mean, sure, everyone has bad days, right? Like if a customer screams at you over a coupon or you get a flat tire on the way to work, you feel bummed out or stressed for a day or two. But it always passed. It never stuck around and turned into this massive, paralyzing weight that just swallowed up my whole personality. So, yeah, no, I've never gone through anything even remotely like this before. This is all completely uncharted territory for me.

inference.note: Ruled out F33.9 because the patient explicitly states this is the first time she has experienced these symptoms and denies any prior history of similar episodes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are specifically tied to the stressor of the promotion or if they persist independently of the work environment.
doctor.question: When you have days off from the restaurant, does this heavy, blank feeling and the inability to do things persist, or do you feel a significant sense of relief and return to your normal self?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I don’t really go for beach walks, bake, garden, or write in my journal much anymore, and when my husband tries to talk with me I mostly just sit there because it feels like I can’t get myself to care or start anything.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the heavy, blank feeling and lack of motivation (which are negative symptoms) persist on days off or if they are just situational to work.

patient.answer:
No, it... it really doesn't go away at all. You'd think it would, right? You'd think, okay, I'm away from the restaurant, I'm away from the buzzing lights and the tickets printing and the customers complaining, so I should just bounce back and feel normal. But I don't. It persists completely. 

Like I was telling you just a minute ago about all those things I used to love? The beach walks, the baking, the gardening, writing in my journal? Those were my day-off activities. That was my whole routine when I wasn't scheduled. But now, when my day off rolls around—like, say it's a Tuesday and I have absolutely nowhere to be—I just wake up and that heavy, blank feeling is already right there, just pinning me down. I don't really go for those beach walks to find sea glass anymore. I don't bake. I don't tend to the garden, and I don't write in my journal much anymore... well, really not at all. It's just this massive wall of nothingness that follows me home. 

And it's almost worse on the days off because that's when my husband is home with me, and like I said, he tries so hard to engage. He'll sit down and try to talk with me, maybe ask what I want to do with our free time or tell me about something he read, and I mostly just sit there. I just sit on the couch because it feels like I absolutely can’t get myself to care or start anything, even on a day when I have literally zero responsibilities. The whole day just slips by. 

It's really frustrating, honestly, because you expect to feel relief on a day off. You expect to be your old self, and when you aren't, when you just sit there staring at the coffee table while your husband is trying to have a normal conversation... it just really shows how stuck I am. So, no, there’s no relief. Whether I'm at the diner or at home on a Sunday, it’s just the same heavy blankness.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms (anhedonia, psychomotor retardation/freezing, persistent low mood, lack of reactivity to the environment) have lasted over 14 months and are consistent with a major depressive episode. The absence of previous episodes makes F32.9 (Major depressive disorder, single episode) more likely than F33.9 (Recurrent), while F43.2 (Adjustment disorder) is less likely given the duration and severity of the symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any periods of abnormally elevated mood, energy, or decreased need for sleep to rule out bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: In your entire life, have you ever experienced a period of several days or weeks where you felt unusually energetic, didn't need much sleep, or felt so 'up' or hyperactive that it was noticeable to others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania or hypomania, such as unusually high energy, decreased need for sleep, or hyperactivity, which are not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I don't... no. I’ve always been someone who really, really needs their sleep. Like, if I don't get at least seven or eight hours, I am just useless the next day. Even back when I was doing those community college classes and working full-time at the other diner, I still slept. I mean, I might have stayed up late a few nights here and there, maybe organizing the apartment, like I mentioned before—I used to have this whole system for my baking supplies, where I'd put all the different flours and sugars into these glass airtight containers and make these cute little chalkboard labels for them so everything looked perfect in the pantry. But even when I did that, I was still exhausted the next day. I'd be dragging my feet through my shift, drinking like three or four cups of black coffee just to keep my eyes open while I was rolling silverware at the back station. 

I never had a time where I just didn't need sleep, or where I felt perfectly fine running on empty. And as for being unusually energetic or, like, hyper... I mean, I was a busy person, sure. Like I said, my husband called me a hummingbird because I liked getting things done. But it wasn't... it wasn't weird or abnormal, you know? It wasn't like I was bouncing off the walls or talking so fast people couldn't understand me. I was just productive. I'd wake up, go to the farmer's market early on a Sunday to get the best heirloom tomatoes and fresh basil from this one specific vendor before they sold out, and then I'd come home and make bruschetta for us... but it was just normal life energy. It wasn't some kind of crazy high where everyone was staring at me. So, no, I've never experienced anything like what you're describing. Never.

inference.note: The patient's report of a persistent, 14-month duration of symptoms (anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, loss of energy, and concentration difficulties) without any history of manic or hypomanic episodes (ruling out F33.9/Bipolar spectrum) supports a diagnosis of a single episode of major depressive disorder. Given the chronicity and severity, it aligns with a major depressive episode.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a pervasive state of anhedonia, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, profound lack of energy (psychomotor retardation), and a sense of 'heavy blankness' that persists across all settings, lasting for over 14 months, consistent with a major depressive episode.
